sources.title: Cover Story: Chris Pratt's Call to Stardom (Vanity Fair, February 2017 issue)
sources.speaker: Chris Pratt, interviewed at home by Rich Cohen
sources.locator: Sections 'Big Time, Small Town' (wrestling, coach anecdote, father's MS, brother and the army), 'Flair for the Dramatic' (coupon sales, Denver office, Maui, Henry), 'The Outsider' (Rae Dawn Chong, Moneyball, Zero Dark Thirty, Guardians audition). The vanityfair.com text and the archive.vanityfair.com copy both end at the paragraph about his guest spot on Mom; nothing after that point was read. Research stage (2026-11-01) re-read the saved vanityfair.com copy for: 'I had everyone convinced I'd been off doing this great sales job'; 'But I was not in a great place'; 'I was always giving away my shifts because I didn't have much overhead'; the Henry passage, including 'It should've made me nervous but didn't'; the coach exchange relayed from Entertainment Weekly and Cohen's follow-up ('I guess that's what I planned to do'); 'Pratt had always wanted to play an action hero but did not think he could pull it off'; 'I was a peculiar kid'.
sources.excerpt: “I’d be devastated,” he said. “Because I put everything into it … “I was like, ‘I don’t know, but I know I’ll be famous and I know I’ll make a shit ton of money.’ ” … a salesman only has one product: himself. “I was great at that,” … I had everyone convinced I’d been off doing this great sales job and making money, and I wasn’t. I had no prospects, no job, was still sort of riding the glory of high school. … ‘I’m more in debt every month. I’m so depressed. I can’t do it.’ … My friends picked me up in a van. They had a cooler of beer. But I was not in a great place. … He said, ‘Jesus told me to talk to you . . .’ At that moment I was like, I think I have to go with this guy. … He says, “Fuck, yeah, I act. Put me in a movie.” … That was the first time I heard someone say, ‘We’re not gonna cast you—you’re too fat.’ So I decided to drop the weight, like in wrestling. … You walk into the room as the character. You let them think the person you are is close to the character they want. You make them think you already are that guy. … He ended up going into the army and told me not to. I think he saw something in me. I was a peculiar kid. … There’s going to be a point in life where you’re going to have to prove that your family is more important to you than show business. … he was a hard man to connect with. … sees it as divinely ordained … That's why I believe in God and the divine … I feel like it was perfectly planned. … That was the carrot Pratt was chasing. It took 15 months, but he finally got it. … One of my best friends heard I'd been floundering. … I was always giving away my shifts because I didn't have much overhead. … It was supposed to be a one-episode deal, a guest spot, but the character took off. Pratt gained weight while shooting the first season—partly because he thought it worked for the character, partly because he'd just been married … If left untreated, it can be devastating, and he left it untreated. … I was very much an individual and happy to be an individual. I dressed funny and was comfortable in my own skin. … I played the room.
sources.context: Long-form cover profile reported while Pratt cooked at his home during a self-declared work break after Guardians of the Galaxy, Jurassic World and Passengers. The high-school coach exchange is Vanity Fair relaying an Entertainment Weekly interview (the EW original refused automated access and was not opened). The Rae Dawn Chong dialogue is Cohen's reconstruction from Pratt's telling. 'A salesman only has one product: himself' is Cohen's paraphrase of Pratt; 'I was great at that' is Pratt's direct quote. The Jim Carrey line is Carrey's advice as Pratt relayed it. The dek ('he sees it as divinely ordained') is Vanity Fair's framing. 'He left it untreated' is Pratt's account of his father's multiple sclerosis, not independent medical record.

sources.excerpt: No one being like a super-confident dumb fat guy.’ So I started. … ’Oh great, I found my niche—this is paying better than the asshole-boyfriend parts.’ … I think I was outwardly having more fun. I was more fun to be around, probably. That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay, was a really fun person to hang around. Now I have less fun. I focus more. … Obnoxious. I was obnoxious, really hyperactive, disruptive...but also Dad was very, very strict, so if I got yelled at, I would stay silent for a long period of time. I was really sensitive. I cried a lot. … I liked making people feel uncomfortable. … he always has to juggle to entertain everybody. And the truth is, Chris didn’t trust himself to just be Chris Pratt—and how desirable that is to an audience. … My bullshit meter’s going off. This screams inauthentic to me. … I knew I was funnier than that stupid fucking director, and he didn’t know what the fuck he was talking about! … I was like the guy holding the purse at events and people just looked right through me. … I hope they fucking audition for Guardians of the Galaxy. … Chris is a man of insights, and he’s always having these big insights—he’s got a new idea every day about everything. … I'm sure I was the first guy in line to buy that line of bullshit … I also understood that there was value to it—my comedic nature understood the irony of a super-happy fat sweaty guy who is completely confident and accepting of who he was. That's fascinating to people. … Why is this guy not crippled with self-doubt? … I don't think Chris Farley did feel that way. … to hide the fact that he didn't feel what he was projecting on the outside. I think that's often the case with comedians. … the highlights of his days were the eating and drinking but that the rest wasn't so good, that he felt physically and mentally sluggish and "didn't feel too great about who I was." … My bones ached, I had cardiovascular issues, I was unhealthy, I was feeling rotten. … I was really sensitive. I cried a lot. I was a crybaby for a long time. … I'm a much more cerebral person than you may expect. … really I'm thinking a lot, in my head below the surface. … Delivery Man, the 2013 Vince Vaughn movie in which Pratt bulked up to 295 pounds for a supporting role
sources.context: Jurassic World-era cover profile. The 'image that I was casting' line answers Heath's question about why Anna Faris may have preferred him heavier; Pratt was joking in part ('I was like a great pet fat guy'). Gunn's remarks describe the first half of the Guardians of the Galaxy shoot, when Pratt overthought his choices. The 'stupid director' line is about early films where his ad-libs were cut and then used. The 'image that I was casting' answer comes directly after Pratt describes the heavy years as physically and emotionally bad ('feeling rotten', 'didn't feel too great about who I was') and compares his cheerful persona to Chris Farley's; it concerns his own offscreen self and interview persona, not the Andy Dwyer character. The 'cerebral person' line is framed by Pratt as what Gunn would say ('I wouldn't want to be quoted [sounding like I was] saying this about myself'). Trap noted 2026-11-01: 'crippled with self-doubt' in the Farley passage is Pratt voicing what onlookers think when they watch Farley ('Why is this guy not crippled with self-doubt? ... I wish I could feel that way'), not a description of himself; it must not be quoted as Pratt's self-report. In the road-rage passage Pratt first repeats his angry version to Heath, then reverses it within the same answer without being challenged.

For me to stand up on the stage and say the things that I said, I'm not sure I touched anybody … If it's like the Westboro Baptist Church, that's different. … Pratt also mentions that he doesn't go to Zoe exclusively. … there's a lot of stuff that people have literally just made up about him—about his politics … I pause here to remind Pratt that none of this noise has hurt his box-office prowess or his reputation in town … she gave me a beautiful, healthy daughter. … That's such a dig at his ex-wife. … My son's gonna read that one day. He's nine. … What happened to the it's-an-honor-just-to-be-nominated-let's-move-on fucking line that we talked about?
sources.context: Cover story reported in Atlanta during Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 filming, timed to Jurassic World Dominion and The Terminal List. Rapkin says the conversation turned to the online backlash 'at his prompting'. The Elliot Page statement text is the 2019 statement as Men's Health quotes it (the original Instagram post was not opened). The Zoe Church film detail is Men's Health's reporting about pastor Chad Veach, not Pratt's statement. 'I cried about it' refers to coverage of an Instagram post about his wife that Pratt feared his son Jack, then nine, would read. The backlash conversation began 'at his prompting'. The tears were over articles reading his 'healthy daughter' Instagram post as a dig at Faris and their premature son, not over faith coverage. Gunn's 'about his politics' remark and the writer's box-office aside are offered as other causes of the online hostility. Attribution: the box-office line is the writer Mickey Rapkin's own aside to Pratt, and Gunn's 'literally just made up' remark was given to Rapkin. Neither appears in the Daily Beast's response (checked against the full Daily Beast text at verify and repair).

sources.excerpt: my father was diagnosed with MS in my sophomore year in high school … And I was like the rookie salesman of the year and got a free trip to Jamaica. … And I was too much of a people pleaser to be a good manager. … it was definitely a failure. … I was that sort of towny guy that like used to be cool and was going to parties. And I just felt like super depressed, you know? … I've been money motivated my whole life because we never had anything … I was the king of my school and I don't have a yearbook because it was $35 and I just wouldn't ask them for that much money. … I work in a business where we create idols and we worship them and no one is worthy of worship. And so not only do we create idols to worship, we create idols to burn. … it doesn't fill the hole inside of my heart that is in a very specific shape that God is the only thing that can fill it. … she's had me say no to things that early in my career, I would have never said no to because they were huge checks. … she's calculated and critical in a way that I'm not. … our priority here is our careers. … I still have a priority of my career being very high, … trying to bring fun and lightheartedness back … I want to get the things right that my dad got right. I want to get the things right that my dad got wrong. … it either instilled in me or potentially revealed a resilience that I had … I sold 500 … So I loved it. … dude, you don't look good. You seem off. And I was off and I was partying a lot … slipping down the wrong path … You're always kind of selling yourself. I always sort of understood how I was seen in the marketplace. … And I didn't have any haters. … yeah, but I don't stand for anything. … I'm completely deferential to whatever the world wants. I'll give you literally anything. Just keep me employed as an actor. … so I stood for something. … I didn't backtrack. … I'm not going to apologize for that. … I don't feel strongly enough about politics to take a stand right now … can I be close to home? … I had a meeting with my manager and agent recently … more of a seriousness … trying to do more comedy, trying to bring fun and lightheartedness back … that's something I have. I mean, I do the animated movies, which are fun … I've been playing this Terminal List character James Reese and then I've been doing some other things, Mercy I did recently … more of a seriousness in some of the roles … I kind of kicked in my door to door sales skills right there
sources.context: Long-form, faith-forward conversation; co-host Ben Sasse has terminal cancer, and Pratt ends by interviewing him. Pratt is the speaker in every quoted passage, identified by first-person biography (Virginia, Minnesota; the Denver office; his father's MS; 'married to... Anna, to Jack's mom'; his manager). A later Sasse remark about his own salesman father is not Pratt's. Two machine transcriptions, not a human listen; the models differ only on filler and spelling ('towny'/'townie'), which should not be quoted. The marketplace passage answers a host question about how he navigated the reaction to his 2018 MTV speech (he notes his first date with Katherine was the next day), so 'up until that point' refers to the years before that speech. In the comedy-plan answer he names his recent roles' seriousness, comedy as 'something I have' and working close to home; he names Mercy as a recent role ('Mercy I did recently') without discussing its reception, and he says he means live-action roles because he already does animated films. The Utah passage answers Sasse's two-part question about keeping 'a gritty, earthy life' rather than becoming 'world stage glitterati', and Pratt opens by crediting God and circumstance. The 'hopelessness' passage sits inside his answer about fame creating 'idols to burn'. The sentence after the 'hole' line ('the people who make it to the top... the chase, the hunt as the excuse to distract myself every day') follows the host's 'That's a profound way that you expressed compassion two minutes ago' and is the host's, not Pratt's.

claims.claim: Asked by GQ whether he discussed his weight with Anna Faris, Pratt said she was "so okay with it" and "Probably in many ways preferred me that way."
claims.inference: Sets up the question his "image" answer responds to.
claims.alternative: It is his guess about her preference, not her statement.

claims.claim: In 2015 Pratt told GQ that in his heavy years 'My bones ached, I had cardiovascular issues, I was unhealthy, I was feeling rotten.'
claims.inference: The health context of the GQ 'image' answer: the heavy years felt bad underneath the outward fun, which is what the cheerful front covered.
claims.alternative: Health alone can explain the later change in his habits without any image motive.

claims.claim: Asked why Anna Faris may have preferred him heavier, Pratt said: 'I think I was outwardly having more fun... That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay, was a really fun person to hang around. Now I have less fun. I focus more.'
claims.inference: In context (GQ 2015) the 'image' is his own offscreen and interview persona in the heavy Parks years, not Andy's happiness. The answer directly follows 'My bones ached... I was feeling rotten' and GQ's report that the highlights of his days were the eating and drinking. Read in that order, 'to convince people that I was okay' admits he was not okay, and the fun was the cover: the Seven pattern of meeting pain with appetite and good cheer. 'Now I have less fun. I focus more' belongs to this health answer, not to the Moneyball story (VF 2017). Limit: one answer, partly joking ('I was like a great pet fat guy').
claims.alternative: The Three reading: a front cast for others with known market value (c-value). Health alone also explains 'less fun'.

claims.claim: GQ records that Pratt laughed and said "I was like a great pet fat guy" right after the image answer.
claims.inference: Shows the answer was delivered partly as a joke.
claims.alternative: The joke may mean the whole answer should be weighted lightly.

claims.claim: GQ reports Pratt saying that during the heavy years he 'didn't feel too great about who I was.'
claims.inference: The phrase sits inside a pain report ('My bones ached, I had cardiovascular issues... feeling rotten'): low self-regard alongside physical misery while the outward fun continued. It is the one motive-level line the Three reading can claim; read in context it is part of what the fun was covering.
claims.alternative: The best motive-level Three clue: a worth problem under the cheerful front. GQ paraphrases most of the sentence and quotes only this phrase.

claims.claim: Pratt told GQ: 'I'm sure I was the first guy in line to buy that line of bullshit,' about the happy-plump-man persona of his comedy years.
claims.inference: He partly believed his own cheerful front; the image was not purely strategic.
claims.alternative: Self-deception about a mask fits the 7 reading as well as the 3 reading.

claims.claim: Pratt compared his persona to Chris Farley's, who in his view 'didn't feel what he was projecting on the outside'.
claims.inference: He frames the cheerful front as covering feelings that did not match it.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest first-person support for the 7 pain-masking reading.

claims.claim: Pratt told GQ: 'I also understood that there was value to it' about the happy-fat-guy persona.
claims.inference: He knew what the persona was worth to audiences, in the same answer as the pain. This is the strongest Three strand in the GQ passage and belongs in 'Why not Type 3?'.
claims.alternative: 'Value' may be comic value: the next words are 'my comedic nature understood the irony'. Knowing what gets laughs is craft in any type.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the GQ answer holds both a front over pain (he bought his own 'line of bullshit', and Farley 'didn't feel what he was projecting') and a front with a price ('there was value to it').
claims.inference: The pain side is in his own words and comes first; the price side is the Three reading's best evidence from the same passage. The profile should show both and argue that the pain side carries the motive.
claims.alternative: The answer may be a single self-deprecating riff, not a motive statement.

claims.claim: Pratt sold coupons door to door from about 18 and says the company had a morning chant, "PMA equals OPM".
claims.inference: Introduces the sales years; his own word for the product is 'attitude', which a Seven's charm and a Three's self-selling can both claim.
claims.alternative: He was 18 to 19 during the job (VF, SmartLess); 'teenage' is approximate at the end of it. His word for what was sold is 'attitude', not 'fun'.

claims.claim: Christopher Michael Pratt was born June 21, 1979, in Virginia, Minnesota; after years in Alaska the family settled in Lake Stevens, Washington, when he was six or seven.
claims.inference: Biographical metadata.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Pratt's first regular TV role was on Everwood (2002 to 2006); his breakthrough role was Andy Dwyer on Parks and Recreation (2009 to 2015); he became a leading man as Star-Lord in Guardians of the Galaxy (2014) and Owen Grady in Jurassic World (2015).
claims.inference: Biographical metadata. The wording follows Wikipedia: Everwood was his 'first regular television role' and Andy Dwyer his 'breakthrough role'.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: The profile reads Pratt as Enneagram Type 7, the Enthusiast, at medium confidence, with Type 3 as the strongest alternative and the wing left open.
claims.inference: Interpretation from repeated choices across 2000-2026 in which pain, failure or limitation was met with pleasure, a good story or the next adventure (see type_hypothesis). Owner decision (DJ, 2026-11-01) names Type 7 as the type under test; the evidence was gathered and tested before confirming it.
claims.alternative: Type 3 (selling himself, marketplace awareness, the hidden sales failure) is the strongest alternative; 8 and 6 have wing-level evidence; 9 explains the deference cluster. Most evidence is self-report in interviews.

claims.claim: Pratt left community college, answered a newspaper ad and sold coupons door to door.
claims.inference: Biographical fact consistent across VF 2017 and Not Dead Yet 2026.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Pratt told Vanity Fair's Rich Cohen that a salesman has only one product, himself (Cohen's indirect report of his words), and said 'I was great at that'.
claims.inference: Early competence at being bought on personal presentation.
claims.alternative: The 'one product' line is Cohen's indirect report ('said Pratt, who told me it didn't really matter what he was selling because a salesman only has one product: himself'). Selling on charm is a Three marker, but the charming pitch is just as much a Seven skill; what separates them is what he did when the selling failed.

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt said the sales job taught him that "regardless of the product you're selling, what you're selling is yourself and you're selling your attitude."
claims.inference: His own statement of the sales lesson: attitude as the product. Part of the Three case; also the Seven's natural pitch. Two transcription models (small.en and large-v3-turbo, 08:08-08:28) agree.
claims.alternative: A general sales lesson many people draw; says nothing by itself about motive.

claims.claim: Pratt says the company chanted 'PMA equals OPM' (positive mental attitude equals other people's money) each morning.
claims.inference: Shows a positivity-as-revenue frame was drilled into him early. Verified with two transcription models (07:05-07:45).
claims.alternative: The frame was the company's, not necessarily his; he calls it terrible.

claims.claim: Pratt called the chant 'terrible' but said it 'either instilled in me or potentially revealed a resilience that I had.'
claims.inference: He credits the job with resilience, not only image-selling. Two models agree (07:15-08:05).
claims.alternative: Resilience under rejection is not type-specific.

claims.claim: Pratt says that in a high-school sales competition classmates sold 17 or 22 cards and he sold 500, and 'So I loved it.'
claims.inference: Competitive selling he enjoyed ('So I loved it'), before any acting. It counts against a Nine reading and is part of the Three case. Two models agree (07:15-08:05).
claims.alternative: A retold brag; the figures are his own and unverified. Enjoying a game you are winning fits a Seven as well.

claims.claim: Vanity Fair reports that Pratt chased the promotion to run his own office for 15 months and got it, outside Denver; he says he 'wasn't even 21.'
claims.inference: A self-initiated, sustained pursuit of the scheme's status prize.
claims.alternative: VF narration ('That was the carrot Pratt was chasing') plus his own age remark.

claims.claim: Retelling the sales venture in 2026, Pratt said he was a great salesman but 'too much of a people pleaser to be a good manager', called it 'definitely a failure', and said that back home, as the former high-school star who 'used to be cool', he felt 'super depressed'.
claims.inference: Consistent across nine years: good at being liked, bad at the parts of management that disappoint people. 'People pleaser' is wing-level material for 6 (or a 9 marker) and argues against core 8.
claims.alternative: 'People pleaser' is also a core self-description of a 2 or a 9. Depression after financial failure at 19 is not type-specific.

claims.claim: Pratt says he told his boss he was in debt and depressed and that his mother sent him a ticket home.
claims.inference: The collapse and its emotional cost, in his words.
claims.alternative: Single retelling of a phone call; Not Dead Yet 2026 corroborates the debt and the flight home.

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt called the sales venture "definitely a failure".
claims.inference: Consistent with the 2017 account.
claims.alternative: Only the shared words of two transcriptions are quoted.

claims.claim: When the sales venture left him in debt and, by his account, depressed, Pratt says he 'had everyone convinced' he was off doing a great sales job and making money, until his mother sent him a ticket home.
claims.inference: Facing failure, he kept up a picture of success for people at home. This is the Three reading's best behavioral evidence outside acting. What he did next decides it: no new venture or image repair, but partying at home and a year of pleasure in Maui (c-friend-off, c-maui-2014, c-giving-shifts).
claims.alternative: Ordinary embarrassment in a 19-year-old, or Seven-style avoidance of a painful truth. 'Everyone' is hyperbole, and it is a single self-report (VF 2017).

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt said he had been "kind of like the star of my hometown" and on returning "just felt like super depressed."
claims.inference: Corroborates the 2017 account of a fall in status felt as depression, nine years apart.
claims.alternative: Depression after financial failure at 19 is not type-specific.

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt said he was partying a lot back home until a friend living in Hawaii saw him and said 'dude, you don't look good. You seem off', and that he was 'slipping down the wrong path'.
claims.inference: After the hidden collapse he was 'partying a lot' and visibly 'off': escape into stimulation, not a push to restore the image. Two models agree (11:30-12:00).
claims.alternative: Partying while depressed after a failure is common in any type at that age.

claims.claim: Interpretation: what Pratt concealed was the outcome; what he did with the bad feeling was party and then leave for Maui.
claims.inference: Labelled in prose as resting on his own retellings (VF 2017; Not Dead Yet 2026), with 'everyone' flagged as exaggeration. The concealment is the Three datum; the response to it is the Seven datum.
claims.alternative: Ordinary embarrassment, or a Three who stalled before finding the next route to success.

claims.claim: Pratt says he has been 'money motivated my whole life because we never had anything', and that although he was 'the king of my school' he has no yearbook because it cost $35 and he 'wouldn't ask them for that much money'.
claims.inference: Scarcity and pride side by side: the star of the school who would not show need. It explains a money drive any type could have. Part of the Three case ('money motivated my whole life'), though in the same answer he says his family were 'total dreamers' with 'no safety net' (c-dreamers).
claims.alternative: Childhood poverty explains a money focus in any type; not asking also fits 2 or 9.

claims.claim: Pratt says he was "the king of my school" but has no yearbook because he would not ask for $35.
claims.inference: Pride and hidden need side by side.
claims.alternative: Not asking also fits 2 or 9; childhood poverty explains it in any type.

claims.claim: In Maui Pratt lived in a van and a tent on the beach and waited tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp.
claims.inference: Biographical; consistent across 2014 and 2017.
claims.alternative: None material.

type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Pratt as a Three: a natural salesman who learned at 18 that 'what you're selling is yourself' (Not Dead Yet 2026), hid a failure behind a success story (VF 2017), built a persona he knew had market value (GQ 2015), remade his body for the roles that paid (VF 2017), read every audition room (VF 2017), and by his own account was 'completely deferential to whatever the world wants' until 2018 (Not Dead Yet 2026). On this reading Maui is a stall before the next route to success (he served Rae Dawn Chong and said 'Put me in a movie'), the fun was the product, and the 2026 comedy turn follows what audiences rewarded ('people really responded well to it', The Playlist 2026). type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does with a bad feeling when no audience needs managing. A Three hides a failure and works harder on the image, because the threat is being seen as worthless; a Seven reframes the pain into a good story or escapes into pleasure, because the threat is being trapped in pain. Pratt's record answers on the Seven side across settings: after the hidden sales failure he partied ('slipping down the wrong path', Not Dead Yet 2026) and spent a year in Maui drinking, smoking weed, working 15 to 20 hours a week and 'always giving away my shifts', then called it 'a charming time' (2014; VF 2017), not a push to restore the image; in the heavy Parks years eating was 'pure euphoria' and 'I did not feel good until I ate again' (Club Random 2025), and he says he bought his own cheerful 'line of bullshit' like Farley, who 'didn't feel what he was projecting' (GQ 2015); a flash of road rage became 'probably my fault... My mind is constantly wandering' within one answer (GQ 2015); he locates hope in the next 'ticket' and says having it all leaves 'a certain brand of hopelessness' (Not Dead Yet 2026, two models); and he says the part he loved was 'a jazz soloist, but not the lead singer... It can be different every time' (The Playlist, October 2026), the opposite of a Three's pull to top billing. Versus 8: 'I am a sensitive person' (MH 2022), 'too much of a people pleaser' (NDY 2026), anger is 'something that I don't do authentically very well' (HSC 2026). Versus 6: he outsources skepticism ('calculated and critical in a way that I'm not') and following a stranger 'should've made me nervous but didn't' (VF 2017). Versus 9: his escapes are stimulation, not withdrawal. Limits: self-report throughout; Maui was at 19 to 20; some lines are caption wording; the jazz-soloist line came while pitching a comedy return.
